title: The Problem of Replication
text:
Scientific claims are only as strong as the evidence that supports them. Before a finding is accepted, it must be replicated by independent teams working under different conditions. Researchers therefore treat a single striking result with considerable caution, however impressive it may appear. Replication, in this sense, is less a formality than the mechanism through which knowledge becomes reliable.

Critics argue that the pressure to publish has made this process less rigorous than it should be. Journals tend to favour novel, positive results, which means that failed experiments are often left unreported. As a consequence, the published literature may present a distorted picture of what is actually known. Many scientists now advocate pre-registering studies, a practice that commits researchers to their methods before the data are collected.

questions.text: According to the first paragraph, what must happen before a scientific finding is accepted?
options: It must be replicated by independent teams.
It must be published in a major newspaper.
It must be approved by a government agency.
It must be tested only once more by its author.

questions.text: What do critics say journals tend to favour?
What can be inferred about the author's attitude toward a single striking result?
options: The author regards it with considerable caution.
The author believes it should be accepted immediately.
The author considers it irrelevant to science.
The author thinks it should be kept secret.

questions.text: Why might pre-registering studies help improve the reliability of published research?
options: It commits researchers to their methods before data are collected, which reduces selective reporting.
It guarantees that all results will be positive.
It removes the need for independent replication.
It allows researchers to change their hypotheses after seeing the data.

vocabulary.definition: repeated by others to check that a result is the same
careful, thorough and strict in method
to prefer or give advantage to something
presented in a way that is not accurate or true

paragraph_translations: Bilimsel iddialar, onları destekleyen kanıt kadar güçlüdür. Bir bulgu kabul edilmeden önce, farklı koşullarda çalışan bağımsız ekipler tarafından tekrarlanmalıdır. Araştırmacılar bu yüzden çarpıcı görünen tek bir sonuca, ne kadar etkileyici olursa olsun, büyük bir temkinle yaklaşırlar. Bu anlamda tekrar, bir formalite olmaktan çok bilginin güvenilir hale geldiği mekanizmadır.

Eleştirmenler, yayın baskısının bu süreci olması gerekenden daha az titiz hale getirdiğini savunuyor. Dergiler yeni ve olumlu sonuçlara eğilim gösterdiği için başarısız deneyler çoğu zaman rapor edilmeden kalıyor. Sonuç olarak yayımlanmış literatür, gerçekte bilinenler hakkında çarpıtılmış bir tablo sunabiliyor. Birçok bilim insanı artık çalışmaların önceden kaydedilmesini savunuyor; bu uygulama, veriler toplanmadan önce araştırmacıları yöntemlerine bağlar.
